summary: Lists requirements for end-to-middle security in SIP. A user agent may not trust all intermediaries to inspect its messages, and may want to protect bodies or headers from them, except those providing services based on content. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When mailing a letter through several post offices, you may want only some of them to read it. This memo lists what is needed to let you choose.

questions: how do you protect messages from some proxies but not others
what is the difference between end-to-end and hop-by-hop security
subtitle: Protecting SIP messages from some intermediaries while letting trusted ones inspect them.

tldr.problem: In SIP calls, messages pass through multiple proxy servers. Some proxies are trusted but some are not. End-to-end encryption blocks all proxies from seeing content, and hop-by-hop encryption lets all proxies see everything. How can a user protect message content from untrusted proxies while letting trusted proxies inspect what they need?
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines requirements for "end-to-middle" security: a UA should be able to encrypt data for trusted intermediaries (proxies) and the far-end receiver, while keeping other intermediaries blocked. This requires allowing selected proxies to decrypt specific message bodies while preventing others from doing so.
tldr.outcome: End-to-middle security would let proxies provide services like location-based routing or content logging, while protecting privacy from proxies that do not need that content. This document lists the requirements for such a mechanism but does not specify a protocol.

today: RFC 4189 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It defines requirements rather than a specific protocol. The SIP community has continued to develop security mechanisms, and various approaches to end-to-middle security have been explored, though a unified standard mechanism remains an open area of development.

sections.title: The Problem: Some Proxies Are Trusted, Some Are Not
sections.content: The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) allows User Agents (phone applications) to set up voice, video, and messaging sessions. Messages pass through proxy servers that route them toward the destination. SIP currently offers two security models: Transport Layer Security (TLS) for hop-by-hop protection (all proxies can decrypt everything), and Secure MIME (S/MIME) for end-to-end protection (only the destination can decrypt). Real-world deployments need a middle ground: some proxies (like the user's home proxy) are trusted with sensitive data, while others (like visiting-network proxies) are not. End-to-middle security would let a UA grant decryption rights to specific trusted proxies without exposing data to untrusted ones.
sections.eli5: Your home phone company (trusted) needs to see some details to route your calls. A random WiFi hotspot (untrusted) should not. The problem is how to let one see something while blocking the other.

sections.title: What End-to-Middle Security Must Cover
sections.content: End-to-middle security encompasses data confidentiality (encryption), data integrity (signatures), and user authentication. The RFC focuses on confidentiality and integrity requirements, since authentication is already handled by existing mechanisms like HTTP Digest authentication and S/MIME signatures. A proxy must be able to verify that a message body comes from an authenticated user, and to verify that the body has not been modified in transit, before it can safely act on the content.
sections.eli5: A trusted proxy needs to know two things: that the data really came from the person who claims to have sent it, and that nobody changed it on the way. The encryption is just one part of the solution.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content: Several SIP services require end-to-middle security. Logging services need to record instant message content but should only run in trusted domains. Location-based routing uses GPS coordinates in the message body to decide where to route a call; a proxy needs this data to route, but untrusted proxies should not see it. User authentication with Authenticated Identity Bodies (AIBs) requires a proxy to decrypt user identity information to verify who is calling. Media-related services, like firewall traversal, need proxies to inspect Session Description Protocol (SDP) data to control firewall rules. In all these cases, the UA must be able to say "Proxy A, please decrypt this body; Proxy B, you cannot."
sections.eli5: Imagine a call-logging service at your home company, location-based routing to find which office you are closest to, or a firewall that needs to know which network ports you will use. All these need a proxy to read part of your message.

sections.title: Requirements for End-to-Middle Mechanisms
sections.content: A solution for end-to-middle security must allow a UA to request that specific proxies verify and/or decrypt selected message bodies. The request itself must be secure: the UA must authenticate its request and provide integrity protection so that proxies know they have not been tricked. The solution should work alongside existing S/MIME end-to-end encryption; if a body is encrypted for the far-end, it should still be possible to encrypt a separate body for a proxy. A UA should be able to discover the security policies of proxies it encounters, so it knows what to disclose and what to protect. The solution should have minimal impact on UAs and proxies that do not use end-to-middle security.
sections.eli5: The mechanism needs to let a UA say "here is proof this request is real, here is the secret for proxy A, but not for proxy B." It should not break existing encrypted calls.

sections.title: Security Risks and Protections
sections.content: End-to-middle security introduces risks. Proxies that can decrypt message bodies become targets for attacks: an attacker could send complicated MIME messages that crash a proxy, or could impersonate a UA and trick a proxy into revealing secrets. Mutual authentication between UAs and proxies is essential, and protection against replay attacks is necessary. Servers must also authenticate each other to prevent one proxy from fooling another. These protections are similar to those provided by TLS for hop-by-hop security.
sections.eli5: If a proxy can read secrets, attackers will try to trick it or crash it. Make sure the proxy can verify that requests are real and that bad actors cannot repeat old messages.
